title: Bellarmine: Christ our righteousness by donated satisfaction
source_text: XXXIV. Quibus consona sunt quae addit ejusdem libri cap. decimo, Resp. ad primum argumentum. Dicitur, inquit, Christus justitia nostra, quoniam satisfecit Patri pro nobis, & eam satisfactionem, ita nobis donat & communicat, quum nos justificat, ut nostra satisfactio & justitia dici possit. Nam etiamsi per justitiam nobis inhaerentem vere justi nominemur & simus, tamen non per eam satisfacimus Deo pro culpa nostra & poena aeterna. Sed est illa justitia inhaerens, cum remissione culpae & sempiternae poenae, effectus satisfactionis Christi, quae nobis in justificatione confertur & applicatur. Et hoc modo non esset absurdum si quis diceret nobis imputari Christi justitiam & merita; cum nobis donentur & applicentur, ac si nos ipsi Deo satisfecissemus: modo non negetur esse in nobis praeterea justitiam inhaerentem, eamque veram & absolutam esse justitiam, cui justo Dei judicio non debeatur poena, sed gloria.
pass_a_gloss: Things consonant with this he adds in chapter ten of the same book, reply to the first argument. Christ is called our righteousness, he says, because he satisfied the Father for us, and so gives and communicates that satisfaction to us when he justifies us that it can be called our satisfaction and righteousness. For although by the righteousness inhering in us we are truly named and are just, yet we do not by it satisfy God for our fault and eternal penalty. But that inherent righteousness, with remission of fault and everlasting penalty, is an effect of Christ’s satisfaction, which is conferred and applied to us in justification. And in this way it would not be absurd if someone said that Christ’s righteousness and merits are imputed to us, since they are given and applied to us as if we ourselves had satisfied God—provided it not be denied that there is besides in us an inherent righteousness, and that it is a true and absolute righteousness to which by God’s just judgment penalty is not due but glory.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine: Christ is our righteousness because his satisfaction is donated as ours in justifying us.
Inherent justice is an effect of that satisfaction; imputation language is fine if inherent justice is not denied.

choices.why: Inherent as effect, not meritorious ground.
